subject: The 6 lines on your inspection report that actually matter
preheader: Roof, electrical, plumbing, foundation, HVAC, mold · how to negotiate vs walk · 3 inspection scenarios

marketSnapshot.headline: Six lines on the inspection report decide everything
marketSnapshot.body: Inspection reports run 30-60 pages. Most of it is documentation and photos. Six specific findings actually decide whether to proceed: roof, electrical, plumbing main lines, foundation, HVAC, and mold/moisture. Everything else (minor caulk gaps, GFCI upgrades, paint chips) is small money. The discipline: skim past the small stuff on first read, focus negotiation on the six that matter.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Negotiate $17k off ask · deal still strong
dealSpotter.body: Inspector flagged: knob-and-tube wiring in attic (~$4,500 remediation), roof at end-of-life (~$8,000), minor foundation settling (cosmetic, $1,500 monitoring + minor fix). Most buyers walk. The smart move: come back with an offer that absorbs $17,000 of the findings into the price. Sellers with property on market past 45-60 days often accept this. Same property, different deal — depends on how you negotiate.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Radon mitigation · sound scarier than it is
dealSpotter.body: Inspection found radon at 6.2 pCi/L (EPA action level is 4.0). Mitigation cost: $1,200-1,500. This is one of those 'sounds scary, costs little' findings — easy to negotiate into the contract. Sellers usually pay for radon mitigation when flagged. If they refuse, you absorb the $1,200 and still have a great deal. Don't let scary-sounding-but-cheap items kill a deal.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Settlement crack with vertical displacement · $12-22k of structural work
dealSpotter.body: Structural engineer review revealed foundation work needed. On a small property, structural fixes can be 10-19% of purchase price. The seller refused to absorb any of it. For an absentee or first-time landlord, this isn't the right project to take on. The headline cap rate evaporated in the inspection. Walk.

blogFeature.title: Property management yes or no — the actual math
blogFeature.excerpt: Good property managers coordinate the inspection-stage rehab work. Self-managers do it themselves. The inspection-stage capex math is where this difference matters most.

qa.question: Six lines decide it — what are they exactly?
qa.answer: (1) Roof — age, condition, life remaining. A roof needing replacement in the next 2-3 years is $8-15k that needs to be in your offer math. (2) Electrical — panel age and amp service, presence of knob-and-tube or aluminum branch wiring. Remediation is a $4-12k surprise. (3) Plumbing — main sewer line condition (camera scope is worth the $300), galvanized vs copper supply lines, water heater age. A failed sewer line is $5-15k. (4) Foundation — any 'structural concerns' note triggers a follow-up structural engineer call ($400-800). Don't proceed without that second opinion. (5) HVAC — age and condition of furnace and AC. A 20-year-old system is end-of-life. (6) Mold/moisture — any active moisture in basements or attics signals systemic issues, not point-fixes. Negotiate offer revisions on the six above. Everything else is small money.
